nameStory: The 'fen' in fen dandelion tells you exactly where to find this rare cousin of the common dandelion - in fens, those special wetlands fed by mineral-rich groundwater. Unlike the dandelions sprouting in every lawn and sidewalk crack, this species chose the challenging life of constantly wet, alkaline soils that most plants can't tolerate.
description: Fen dandelion is a small, specialized wetland plant that looks remarkably similar to the common dandelion most people know from their yards. This perennial herb grows low to the ground in a rosette pattern, typically reaching only 4-8 inches tall. **[UNCERTAIN: Exact size range]** It produces the classic yellow, composite flower heads that dandelions are famous for, but you'll only find it in very specific wetland habitats rather than disturbed areas.

habitat: Fen dandelion grows exclusively in alkaline fens, calcareous wetlands, and mineral-rich marshy areas throughout New England. These specialized habitats are fed by groundwater rich in calcium and other minerals, creating constantly moist, alkaline conditions. You'll often find it growing alongside sedges, wild iris, and other fen specialists in areas that stay wet year-round.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge early and flower buds begin forming as soon as the soil warms, typically blooming from late spring into early summer.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flowers followed by the familiar white, fluffy seed heads that disperse on the wind.
seasonality.fall: Leaves remain green longer than many wetland plants, gradually yellowing as temperatures drop and new rosettes establish.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, surviving as roots and potentially small basal leaf clusters protected under snow and ice.

funFact: With only 2 recorded observations in all of New England, fen dandelion is so rare that you're more likely to spot a moose in your backyard than find this elusive wetland specialist - making any discovery a genuine botanical treasure hunt victory!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common dandelion, but habitat is the dead giveaway - if you're in a lawn, field, or disturbed area, it's definitely the common species. Fen dandelion only grows in pristine alkaline wetlands. The red-seeded dandelion also prefers different habitats and has distinctive reddish seed characteristics.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'dandelion,' many people don't realize there are actually multiple dandelion species, each adapted to different environments. The fen dandelion represents nature's specialist approach - trading the ability to grow anywhere for the advantage of thriving in a habitat most plants find impossible.
compareHints: Fen dandelion differs from common dandelion primarily in its exclusive wetland habitat and potentially smaller, more delicate features. **[UNCERTAIN: Physical differences]** Unlike red-seeded dandelion, which prefers dry, sandy soils, or cinnamon-fruited dandelion found in northern rocky areas, fen dandelion is strictly a wetland species. The habitat requirement is so specific that location alone usually confirms identification.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common dandelion is much more widespread than its relatives in New England.
Red-seeded dandelion is most easily distinguished from common dandelion by its reddish seeds rather than pale yellow ones.
Among New England dandelions, only the cinnamon-fruited dandelion has distinctly brown seeds - common dandelion and red-seeded dandelion both have much paler, straw-colored to light brown fruits.
